name: Muller's Ratchet
statement: Without sex to reset it, a genome can only accumulate damage, never shed it.
statementAccent: only accumulate damage, never shed it
meaning: In an asexual population, harmful mutations build up irreversibly. Each time chance eliminates the individuals carrying the fewest mutations, that cleanest class cannot be rebuilt without recombination, so the minimum mutational load clicks up a notch, and, like a ratchet, can only turn one way.
mechanism: New deleterious mutations arise each generation, and selection removes them imperfectly. In a finite population, genetic drift can wipe out the least-mutated class (the fittest individuals) simply because it is small and happens to leave no offspring. Because asexual offspring carry at least as much load as their parents, that lost class cannot be regenerated except by rare back-mutation, so the new minimum becomes the next click. Sexual recombination halts and reverses the ratchet by reassembling a low-load genome from the good portions of two more-mutated parents, which is why the mechanism is a leading explanation for why sex exists.

examples.text: Obligately asexual lineages tend to be evolutionarily short-lived, their genomes decaying toward extinction: with the ancient asexual bdelloid rotifers standing as a much-discussed apparent exception.

The mammalian Y does not recombine over most of its length and has degenerated across evolutionary time, losing most of its ancestral genes: a ratchet-like decay, echoed in non-recombining mitochondrial genomes.
A small population feels stronger drift, so the ratchet clicks faster: a concern in conservation genetics, and related to the mutational meltdown that can spiral small populations toward extinction.

variants.name: Mutational meltdown
variants.text: Lynch and Gabriel's accelerating spiral: ratchet-driven load shrinks the population, which strengthens drift, which turns the ratchet faster, hastening extinction.

variants.name: The evolution of sex
variants.text: The broader question the ratchet speaks to: recombination's ability to reconstitute the least-loaded genotype is a leading candidate for why sexual reproduction is maintained.

whyItMatters: It is a rigorous population-genetic argument for one of the deepest advantages of sex: recombination can undo mutational decay that asexual reproduction cannot. It illuminates the degeneration of Y chromosomes and organelle genomes and the fragility of small, non-recombining populations.

working.text: where recombination is absent (asexual lineages, the Y chromosome, mitochondria) expect deleterious mutations to accumulate over time.
since drift drives the ratchet, expect faster mutational decay in small, isolated populations, a real conservation concern.

working.lead: Note that even rare sex helps
working.text: occasional recombination, gene conversion, or gene transfer can arrest the ratchet, so a little mixing goes a long way.

limits: The ratchet turns fastest under small population size, high deleterious mutation rate, and little or no recombination; in large populations with a well-populated zero-mutation class it turns very slowly or effectively stalls. Rare back-mutations and, more importantly, compensatory or beneficial mutations can halt or even reverse the accumulation, and even occasional recombination arrests it. Its quantitative importance and click-rate are debated and model-dependent, hinging sensitively on selection coefficients, epistasis, and effective population size.
misreadings: It does not say asexual lineages must quickly die: the ratchet can turn imperceptibly slowly in large populations, and beneficial mutations can offset it. And it is not a claim that mutations are irreversible in principle, only that the cleanest genotype, once lost by chance, cannot be reassembled without recombination.
origin: The concept is due to Hermann J. Muller, who argued in 1932 and more fully in 'The relation of recombination to mutational advance' (Mutation Research 1(1):2-9, 1964) that asexual genomes cannot efficiently purge harmful mutations; the term 'Muller's ratchet' was coined by Joe Felsenstein in 1974.

sources.text: Muller's ratchet, Wikipedia. — the irreversible-accumulation mechanism, the link to the evolution of sex, and the Muller/Felsenstein attribution.
Muller, H. J. "The relation of recombination to mutational advance," Mutation Research 1(1):2-9 (1964), PubMed. — the original argument.
